title: A car for every Indian family
hook: A failed car company, no car experts, and a huge goal. Can you build India's first family car?

profit.label: Sales
profit.hint: Cars made and money coming in today

future.label: Future
future.hint: How strong Maruti will be in the years ahead

intro.text: Gurgaon, 1981. Ten years ago, a company on this land promised Indians a small car of their own, but it made only a handful of cars before it was shut down. Now the government is trying again with a new company, Maruti Udyog, and it has put you in charge.

s_goal.text: Your goal is 1 lakh cars a year, while all of India buys fewer than 40,000, nearly all of them big, old Ambassadors and Padminis. Nobody on your team has ever built a car, so first you need a foreign carmaker that can show you how.

d1.title: Find a partner
d1.setup: Fiat, Volkswagen, Renault, Peugeot and Nissan have all said no, and most other carmakers want to send their own people to run the plant. Daihatsu of Japan has been your best hope for months, but now a message shows it plans to build its car with another Indian firm. A few days later, a message arrives from Suzuki, a smaller Japanese maker. It wants in.
d1.question: Who do you build India's car with?
d1.advisor: The last Maruti made promises and no cars, so we cannot move slowly. But this partner will shape the company for years.

options.label: Keep pushing Daihatsu. The talks are far along, but its last message was cold.
options.outcome: You push Daihatsu for months, and late in the year it agrees to help. But India is a side project for it, so it sends only a small team, and you are behind before the first machine arrives.
options.why: Remember: own your core skill, and get help with the rest. Maruti's core was learning to build cars, so it needed a partner keen to teach. Daihatsu was not keen, so it sent little help, and you lost months finding that out.
options.better: Go with the partner that comes to you hungry, even if it is smaller and less famous.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you waited on a partner that had stopped caring.

options.label: Open talks with Suzuki. It came to you, but it is small and unknown in India.
options.outcome: Talks begin in April 1982. Suzuki's president meets your team himself, and his money offer is the best you get. On 2 October 1982 you sign, and Suzuki buys about a quarter of Maruti, with a plan to own more later.
options.why: Remember: own your core skill, and get help with the rest. Maruti's core was learning to build cars in India. Suzuki was keen to teach, and your people went to Japan to learn, so the know-how stayed with Maruti.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you picked the hungry partner over the famous one.

options.label: Sign with a maker that will run the plant itself. It's fast, but its people decide.
options.outcome: A foreign maker signs quickly and flies in its own managers and machines. Work starts fast, but your Indian staff are kept at the side, watching, while every big decision is made far away.
options.why: Remember: own your core skill, and get help with the rest. Building cars was the one skill Maruti had to own. When a partner runs everything, you end up with a factory but none of the know-how.
options.better: Pick a partner that will train your own people and help Indian suppliers grow.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you bought a factory instead of learning to build one.

d2.title: Which car first?

setup.text: Suzuki makes three vehicles you could build: a tiny four-seat car, a small van and a light jeep. A survey shows that 9 in 10 car trips in India carry four people or fewer, mostly inside cities. But one of your board members says Maruti should make vans and trucks, not cars.

Daihatsu makes three vehicles you could build: a tiny four-seat car, a small van and a light jeep. A survey shows that 9 in 10 car trips in India carry four people or fewer, mostly inside cities. But one of your board members says Maruti should make vans and trucks, not cars.

Your partner offers three vehicles you could build: a tiny four-seat car, a small van and a light jeep. A survey shows that 9 in 10 car trips in India carry four people or fewer, mostly inside cities. But one of your board members says Maruti should make vans and trucks, not cars.

d2.question: What do you build first?
d2.advisor: If we build all three, every kind of buyer has a reason to come to us. If we build only one, we must guess right the first time.

options.label: Build only the small car. It's the cheapest to buy and run, but it's tiny.

outcome.text: You pick a car based on Suzuki's 1979 Alto, with a small 796 cc engine, and call it the Maruti 800. Front-wheel drive and disc brakes will be new to Indian buyers.
Your partner's small car is light and cheap to run, which is just what city families need, although it will take work to make it ready for Indian roads.

options.why: Remember: every extra model adds hidden costs. One car meant one set of parts, one line and one kind of training. It was also the car most families could afford, and the van and jeep could follow later.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you built one car, the one most families could use and afford.

options.label: Build all three at once, so every kind of buyer finds a Maruti to suit them.
options.outcome: Your new plant must now learn three vehicles at once: three sets of parts, three sets of tools and three kinds of training. Every line moves slowly, and the December date starts to slip.
options.why: Remember: every extra model adds hidden costs. Three vehicles meant three times the parts to find and the skills to learn, in a plant that had never built even one.
options.better: Build one vehicle well first, the small car, and add the others once the plant runs smoothly.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you tried to build three vehicles before you could build one.

options.label: Build the van first. It fits a big family and a shop's goods, but costs more.
options.outcome: Shopkeepers and taxi owners will like the van. But a family on a scooter still won't be able to buy a car, and that is why Maruti was started.
options.why: Remember: every extra model adds hidden costs, so start with one, and make it the one most buyers need. You picked one, but the van mostly served shops and taxis. India's biggest gap was a car a family could afford.
options.better: Build the small car first, and add the van soon after.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you started with a useful van, but missed the biggest need.

text.text: The launch is set for December 1983, but your plant is learning three vehicles at once. You still need hundreds of Indian firms to make parts, and dealers across the country.

The launch is set for December 1983. In just 14 months you must build a factory, find hundreds of Indian firms to make parts, and sign up dealers across the country. Your people fly to Japan to learn how Suzuki does it.
The launch is set for December 1983, and Daihatsu's slow start has eaten into your time. You still need a factory, hundreds of Indian firms to make parts, and dealers across the country.
The launch is set for December 1983. Your partner's managers are building the factory fast, and they want to bring almost every part from abroad. You still need dealers across the country.

d3.title: Make the date
d3.setup: The Indian parts makers are not ready. Their quality is uneven and their parts often arrive late. If you wait for them, there will be no car in December.
d3.question: How do you make the launch date?
d3.advisor: If we miss the date, people will say Maruti has failed again. But if everything comes from abroad, how Indian is our car?

options.label: Wait until Indian parts makers are ready, even if the launch slips a year.
options.outcome: December comes and goes with no car. The papers start calling Maruti another failed dream, and Delhi starts asking hard questions.
options.why: Remember: find the longest chain of work, and buy in whatever would make you late. Indian parts were that chain, so waiting for them made the whole launch wait.
options.better: Launch on time with imported parts, and set firm dates for switching to Indian ones.
options.takeaway: In 1983 you put a perfect car ahead of an on-time car.

options.label: Use Indian parts as they are today. You keep the date, but quality is uneven.
options.outcome: You make the date with an all-Indian vehicle. But within weeks, buyers are back at the dealers with leaks, rattles and breakdowns, and they say the new Maruti is no better than the old cars.
options.why: Remember: buy in whatever would make you late, then learn to make it. You kept the date with parts that were not ready, and a car built from them broke down in front of everyone.
options.better: Use proven imported parts at first, and raise Indian suppliers to the new standard step by step.
options.takeaway: In 1983 you chose a local label over real quality.

options.label: Launch with parts shipped from Japan, and promise to go Indian within five years.

outcome.text: Your workers put together kits shipped from Japan. When the first 192 cars roll out in December 1983, only the tyres and the batteries are Indian, less than 3% of the car. You promise 95% within five years.
You put together parts shipped from abroad. Very little of the vehicle is Indian yet, but you now have a firm plan to change that.

options.why: Remember: find the longest chain of work, and buy in whatever would make you late. Indian parts were on that chain. Imported kits kept the date, and a firm five-year plan meant you would still make the parts yourself.
options.takeaway: In 1983 you launched on time and made a firm plan to go local.

text.text: 14 December 1983, New Delhi. The Prime Minister, Indira Gandhi, hands the keys of the first Maruti 800 to its owner, an Indian Airlines employee who paid ₹47,500. The plant, the suppliers and the dealers were all built in 14 months.
Your first vehicles rolled out on time in December 1983, but the repair bills are growing, and so are the jokes about Maruti.
December 1983. Your first vehicle rolls out of Gurgaon on time, with the press watching. Now you will find out how many people want one.
Late 1984. Almost a year behind plan, your first vehicle finally rolls out of Gurgaon, and this one is mostly Indian. People are glad to see it, but many had stopped believing it would ever come.
1984. Months behind plan, your first vehicles finally roll out of Gurgaon. Learning three vehicles at once slowed every line, and the papers have started to joke about Maruti.

d4.title: How will the plant work?

setup.text: About 1,20,000 people have booked a car, but this year you can make only about 20,000. More machines need foreign money, and India has very little to spare. So every extra car must come from the plant you already have.

Far more people have booked than you can supply. Delhi now wants your own managers to run the shop floor, not your partner's. More machines need foreign money that India lacks, so every extra car must come from this plant.
Far more people have booked than you can supply this year. More machines need foreign money, and India has very little to spare. So every extra car must come from the plant you already have.

d4.question: How will you run the plant?
d4.advisor: Our shop heads know Indian workers, and each has his own way. The partner's way is strict, and it treats a manager just like a worker.

options.label: Trust your experienced shop heads to run their shops in their own way.
options.outcome: Each shop runs its own way. The weld shop and the paint shop check cars differently, a car that passes one shop fails the next, and nobody can say which way is right. Output creeps up slowly.
options.why: Remember: one standard way of working cuts cost and errors. Six ways of working meant six kinds of mistakes, and no way to learn which way worked best.
options.better: Pick one way for every job, write it down, and train everyone in it, bosses included.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you let every shop work its own way.

options.label: Run every shop the partner's way, with one set of rules. Managers lose their perks.

outcome.text: Officers and workers eat the same food in one canteen and work in open offices. Shifts start with exercises, tea breaks are short, and nobody leaves dust on the floor. Training never stops, and in 1984–85 Gurgaon beats its target of 20,000 cars.

Bosses and workers follow the same rules, from the first exercise of the shift to the last check on the line. Every worker is trained in the same way, and month by month more cars roll out right first time.

options.why: Remember: one standard way of working cuts cost and errors. When every shop and every rank works the same way, a mistake shows up fast, and every fix reaches everyone.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you ran the whole plant one standard way, bosses included.

options.label: Add a second shift of new workers now. They'll learn the job on the line.
options.outcome: More cars roll out, but each new worker copies whoever stands beside them. Small faults creep in, and more cars come back to dealers to be fixed.
options.why: Remember: one standard way of working cuts cost and errors. More hands helped, but with no single way to learn, every new worker learned a slightly different job.
options.better: Set one standard way first, train everyone in it, then add the shift.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you added hands before you had one way of working.

d5.title: Build Indian suppliers

setup.text: Less than a tenth of each car is made in India so far, and every imported part costs foreign money. To keep your promise, hundreds of small Indian firms must learn to make much better parts, and fast.
Your Indian parts break too often, and buyers are angry. Hundreds of Indian firms must learn to make much better parts, or your vehicles will never be trusted.
Your partner's managers want to keep buying from their own suppliers abroad, and every imported part costs foreign money. Hundreds of Indian firms are waiting for a chance.
Your Indian suppliers are making parts now, but their quality is uneven, and hundreds of them must learn to work to a higher standard.
Too many parts still come from abroad, and every one costs foreign money. Hundreds of Indian firms must learn to work to a higher standard.

d5.question: How do you choose your suppliers?
d5.advisor: If we choose only a few firms, many people will be angry with us. If we choose many, can any of them get good?

options.label: Pick a few firms on quality alone, and push them hard. Most local firms get nothing.

outcome.text: A powerful politician asks to become a supplier. Your supplier team tells him to bring a sample and be tested like everyone else, and he never comes back. Hundreds of firms have to change their machines and their habits, and once it is clear that Maruti will not fail, they take it seriously.
You hold every supplier to one standard, and you test them all, even the well-connected ones. It is slow and painful, but parts start arriving on time and fitting right.

options.why: Remember: pick a few strong suppliers on quality, and push them. Big orders gave those firms a reason to buy better machines and learn, so the car got cheaper, more Indian and better.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you chose a few strong suppliers on merit and pushed them hard.

options.label: Give orders to many small firms in every state. Each firm's order will be small.
options.outcome: Politicians in every state are happy, and hundreds of firms get a start. But each one makes too few parts to get good at it, so quality stays uneven and costs stay high.
options.why: Remember: pick a few strong suppliers on quality, and push them. With orders spread thin, no firm made enough parts to pay for better machines or to learn properly.
options.better: Pick a few strong firms on quality alone, give them big orders and train them hard.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you spread your orders thin and nobody got good.

options.label: Buy most parts from abroad for now. Quality is safe, but it costs foreign money.
options.outcome: Quality stays high, but each car eats up scarce foreign money, Delhi grows impatient, and Indian suppliers never get their chance to grow.
options.why: Remember: pick a few strong suppliers on quality, and push them to get better. Buying abroad kept quality safe, but it built no Indian supplier, used up foreign money and broke your promise to go local.
options.better: Choose Indian suppliers on quality alone and help them improve, so the car becomes Indian step by step.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you played safe with imports and built no local strength.

text.text: It is 1987, and Maruti is growing up fast. A van joined the 800 in 1984 and the Gypsy jeep came in 1985. In 1986 the 1,00,000th Maruti rolled out, and the 800 got a newer body. Yet the queue at home is still years long.
It is 1987. Your parts now come from all over India, but quality is uneven, and many small firms can't keep up with your orders.
It is 1987. Your cars sell, but each shop still works its own way, and faults that one shop fixes keep coming back in another.
It is 1987. The extra shift made more cars, and you are slowly teaching everyone one way of working, but the repair bills from those early months still hurt.
It is 1987. Your vehicles are on Indian roads, and people are still queuing for them. Now you have to decide how far to push Maruti.

d6.title: Sell abroad?

setup.text: Buyers at home are still queuing, so you could sell every car you make in India. Suzuki and the head of your board both say you should not try to sell abroad.
Buyers at home are still queuing, so you could sell everything you make in India. Your partner and the head of your board both say you should not try to sell abroad.

d6.question: What do you do next?
d6.advisor: Europe pays in foreign money, which we badly need. But if we fail there, every paper in India will say so.

options.label: Stay in India. Every car you make already sells, and your partner agrees.
options.outcome: Sales stay strong. But with no tough buyers to answer to, quality improves slowly, and when rivals arrive years later, you are less ready than you should be.
options.why: Remember: tough buyers make you better, so seek them out. With a long queue at home, nobody pushed you to improve.
options.better: Sell some cars abroad to learn from tougher buyers, even while the queue at home is long.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you stayed home and missed a chance to raise your game.

options.label: Send a third of your cars to Europe for foreign money, though the queue grows.
options.outcome: Thousands of cars sail for Europe, and the queue at home grows by years. Many need changes to pass Europe's rules, so they wait at the port while your engineers fix them. Families at home ask why foreigners drive Marutis first.
options.why: Remember: tough buyers make you better, so seek them out, but start small so you can learn. A small batch would have taught you the same lessons without making every Indian buyer wait longer.
options.better: Send a small first batch abroad to learn, and grow exports as your plant gets better.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you bet a third of your cars on buyers you had never met.

options.label: Send a small first batch to Europe, against the advice of your partner and board.

outcome.text: You ship 500 cars to Hungary, and the first ones arrive on 24 October 1987. France follows in 1989 and the Netherlands in 1990. To sell in Europe, the 800 gets seat belts, which it never had before.
Selling abroad pushes your plant and your suppliers toward world standards, and buyers in other countries start to notice your vehicles.

options.why: Remember: tough buyers make you better, so seek them out. Europe's buyers and rules pushed you to raise your standards, and a small first batch kept the risk small.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you went abroad to get better, not just bigger.

text.text: By 1988 Gurgaon can make 1,00,000 cars a year, the goal you were given in 1981. The 800 stays on sale until 2014, and nearly 29 lakh are built. In 2024, about 4 in every 10 cars sold in India are still Marutis.
You built the people's car, one standard way of working and a strong group of Indian suppliers around it. For millions of families, a Maruti becomes their first car.

survivor.title: A good company, a smaller dream

text.text: Maruti makes three good vehicles, but none of them early or cheap enough. It never becomes the family car of India, and when foreign rivals arrive in the 1990s, they take that prize.
Maruti's vans are everywhere, carrying goods and families. But the small family car comes late, and when foreign rivals arrive in the 1990s, Maruti is a strong player, not the clear leader.
Maruti makes good cars and good money, but it never becomes the car of every Indian family. When foreign rivals arrive in the 1990s, it is a strong player, not the clear leader.

collapse.title: Another failed dream
collapse.text: The vehicles cost too much or break too often, and Indian suppliers never grow. Like the first Maruti, the company becomes the story of a big promise that did not come true.

fired.title: Delhi lets you go
fired.text: Delhi has seen enough. After three costly calls, the government, which owns Maruti, gives your job to someone else, and the people's car must wait for a new boss.

realHistory: In 1981 the government started Maruti Udyog, a company with no car experience. In October 1982 it signed with Suzuki, a late but eager partner, and in just 14 months it built a factory in Gurgaon, a group of suppliers and a dealer network. The first Maruti 800 was handed over on 14 December 1983. About 1,20,000 people booked in the first year, far more than Maruti could make. It ran its plant the Japanese way, with one canteen and open offices for officers and workers alike. Maruti pushed hundreds of Indian suppliers to raise their quality, began exporting to Europe in 1987, and could make 1,00,000 cars a year by 1988. The 800 stayed on sale until 2014, and Maruti Suzuki is still India's biggest carmaker.
